cards.title: Forms of learning & generalisation
cards.hook: Learning = improving performance from data. The feedback type defines the learning type.
cards.visual:
TypeFeedbackExample
Supervisedlabelled input-output pairsspam classifier, house price
Unsupervisednone, find structureclustering
Reinforcementrewards and punishmentsgame playing
example: Degree-12 polynomial through all points → overfits.
cards.trap: i.i.d. = independent AND identically distributed; both parts matter.
explain: Machine learning means a program gets better at a task by learning from data instead of being told the rules. What kind of learning it is depends on what feedback the data gives:

Supervised learning: every example comes with the correct answer (a label). Like a student with a worked-answer book: show photos labelled 'cat' or 'dog' and it learns a function h(x) that maps inputs to outputs, then predicts labels for new photos.
Unsupervised learning: no answers at all. The program must find structure on its own, e.g. grouping customers into clusters with similar buying habits.
Reinforcement learning: no answer per example, only rewards or punishments after actions (win or lose a game). The agent learns which actions lead to high reward over time.
Within supervised learning: if the output is a category (sunny/cloudy/rainy, COVID positive/negative) it is classification; if it is a number (house price, temperature) it is regression.
Learning assumes the data is i.i.d.: examples are independent of each other and come from the same distribution, so the future looks like the past.

Generalisation = doing well on NEW data. A degree-12 polynomial through every training point overfits: it memorises noise and predicts badly. Ockham's razor: choose the simplest hypothesis that fits the data.

tex.t: \text{Data } (x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_N,y_N) \text{ with } y = f(x); \text{ learn } h \approx f
where: a new input; predict y = h(x)

cards.title: Confusion matrix and classification metrics
cards.hook: Accuracy alone can lie; precision and recall tell you which mistakes you make.
cards.memory: Precision = Predicted row; Recall = Real (actual) column.
cards.trap: Lecture 4 puts PREDICTED on the rows; some textbooks swap them. Read the labels.
explain: A confusion matrix counts four kinds of outcome. In Lecture 4, rows are what the model PREDICTED and columns are what is ACTUALLY true.
TP: said positive, really positive. FP: said positive, really negative (false alarm). FN: said negative, really positive (a miss). TN: said negative, really negative.
Accuracy = fraction of all predictions that are right. It can mislead: if 99% of emails are not spam, always saying 'not spam' scores 99%.

Precision asks: when the model says positive, how often is it right? Use it when false alarms are costly. Recall asks: of all real positives, how many did it catch? Use it when misses are costly (cancer screening).
F1 combines precision and recall (their harmonic mean). ROC plots TPR against FPR for every threshold; AUC is the area under it (1 = perfect, 0.5 = random guessing).

cards.title: Regression metrics
cards.hook: How far off are numeric predictions, and in what way?
cards.visual:
MetricRangeBetterNote
MAE[0, ∞)lowersame units, robust
MSE[0, ∞)lowersquares errors
RMSE[0, ∞)lowersame units, penalises large errors
R²(−∞, 1]highercan be negative
MAPE[0, ∞) %lowerfails when y ≈ 0
cards.memory: MAE = Absolute, MSE = Squared, RMSE = Root-squared.
cards.trap: Forgetting to divide by n, or squaring the sum instead of summing the squares.
explain: Regression metrics measure how far numeric predictions are from the truth. Each one looks at the errors y − ŷ differently.
MAE: average size of the error, ignoring sign. Easy to read ('on average we're off by $20,000').
MSE: average of SQUARED errors. Squaring makes big mistakes count much more. RMSE = √MSE brings it back to the original units.
R²: how much better than just predicting the average. 1 = perfect, 0 = no better than the mean, negative = worse than the mean.
MAPE: average error as a percentage of the true value. Scale-free, but breaks when true values are 0 or near 0.

cards.title: Workflow, k-fold CV and avoiding leakage
cards.hook: Tune on training data only; touch the test set once.
formula: try every parameter combination with k-fold CV
refit on the full training set
example: Split 80/20 → tune max_depth by 5-fold CV on the 80% → retrain best → evaluate once on the 20% → deploy & monitor drift.
cards.trap: Tuning hyperparameters on the test set = data leakage.
explain: To get an honest score you must test on data the model has never seen. So you split off a test set first and lock it away.

To choose settings (hyperparameters such as tree depth) you use k-fold cross-validation on the training set only: split it into k folds, train on k − 1 and validate on the remaining one, rotate, and average the k scores.
Pick the best settings, retrain on the full training set, then evaluate ONCE on the test set. Using the test set to tune is data leakage and gives an over-optimistic score.

cards.title: Ensembles: random forest and gradient boosting
cards.hook: Many weak learners combined beat one strong-looking tree.
cards.visual:
Random forest (bagging)Gradient boosting
Trees builtindependently, in parallelsequentially
Each tree seesbootstrap sample + random featuresresidual/gradient of current errors
Combinevote (class) / average (regression)sum of tree contributions
Main benefitreduces variancereduces bias, strong on tabular data
Watch outslower with many treesoverfits with too many trees; small learning rate needs more trees
example: A single deep tree overfits → random forest averages 100 trees → lower variance.
cards.memory: Bagging = Bag of independent trees; Boosting = each tree Boosts the last one's weak spots.
cards.trap: Boosting learners are DEPENDENT (sequential); bagging learners are not.
explain: An ensemble asks many models and combines their answers, like asking a crowd instead of one person.

Random forest (bagging): grow many decision trees, each on a random bootstrap sample of the rows and random subsets of features. They vote (classification) or average (regression). Independent trees make different mistakes that cancel out, so variance drops.
Gradient boosting: grow trees one after another; each new tree fixes the errors left by the previous ones. The final prediction is the sum of all the small corrections, scaled by a learning rate.

cards.title: Linear regression and gradient descent
cards.hook: Gradient descent walks downhill on the loss surface.
cards.visual:
QuantityValue
Modelh_w(x) = w₁x + w₀
LossΣ (y − (w₁x + w₀))²
Updatewᵢ ← wᵢ − α ∂Loss/∂wᵢ
Per examplew₀ ← w₀ + α(y − h); w₁ ← w₁ + α(y − h)x
formula: learning rate (step size), fixed or decaying
gradient descent reaches the global minimum
cards.trap: Adding α×gradient (instead of subtracting) climbs the loss.
explain: Linear regression fits a straight line ŷ = w₁x + w₀. We want the line with the smallest total squared error (loss).

Gradient descent finds it by walking downhill on the loss surface: compute the slope (gradient) of the loss for each weight and take a small step the OPPOSITE way. The step size α is the learning rate.
Too large α overshoots and can diverge; too small α is slow. Because this loss is convex (a bowl), gradient descent reaches the global minimum.

tex.t: w_0 \leftarrow w_0 + \alpha\,(y - h_w(x)) \qquad w_1 \leftarrow w_1 + \alpha\,(y - h_w(x))\,x

cards.title: Logistic regression and cross-entropy
cards.hook: Squash a linear score into a probability with a sigmoid.
cards.trap: Logistic regression is a CLASSIFIER despite the name.
explain: Logistic regression is a CLASSIFIER. It computes a linear score z = w·x, then squashes it through the sigmoid into a probability between 0 and 1.
It's trained with binary cross-entropy, which punishes confident wrong answers very heavily (p = 0.99 for a true 0 gives loss ≈ 4.6).
The gradient is beautifully simple: (p − y) × input.

cards.title: K-nearest neighbours
cards.hook: Tell me who your neighbours are, I'll tell you who you are.
cards.memory: No training, all memory: KNN is instance-based (non-parametric).
cards.trap: Not scaling features lets one large-range feature dominate the distance.
explain: KNN doesn't build a model. To predict for a new point, it finds the k most similar training points (closest by distance) and lets them decide.
Classification: majority vote of the k neighbours. Regression: average of their values.
Because it is all about distance, features must be scaled; otherwise a feature measured in thousands drowns out one measured in units.

tex.t: d(\mathbf x, \mathbf q) = \sqrt{\sum_i (x_i - q_i)^2} \qquad \hat y = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j \in N_k(\mathbf q)} y_j

cards.title: Support vector machines
cards.hook: Draw the separating line with the widest possible street.
formula: + C Σξᵢ; large C punishes errors more
cards.memory: Only the points on the street edges (support vectors) matter.
cards.trap: Large C = narrower margin, fewer violations (risk of overfitting); too high RBF gamma = wiggly boundary.
explain: An SVM draws the separating line (hyperplane) that leaves the widest possible gap between the two classes, like the widest street you can drive between two groups of houses.
Only the points touching the edges of the street matter; they are the support vectors. A wide margin tends to generalise well.

Soft margin: allow a few points inside the street, paying a penalty C for each. Large C = strict (narrow street, fewer errors), small C = relaxed. Kernels let the SVM draw curved boundaries by implicitly mapping the data into a higher-dimensional space.

tex.t: \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b = 0, \qquad f(\mathbf x) = \operatorname{sign}(\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b), \qquad \text{margin} = \frac{2}{\lVert \mathbf w\rVert}
\min_{\mathbf w, b}\; \tfrac12 \lVert \mathbf w\rVert^2 \;\text{ s.t. }\; y_i(\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x_i + b) \ge 1
K(\mathbf x,\mathbf z) = (\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z + 1)^p \qquad K(\mathbf x,\mathbf z) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert\mathbf x - \mathbf z\rVert^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
